about.title: Elk Grove Slip & Fall and Premises Liability Claims
about.longDescription: Elk Grove has grown into a city of nearly 167,000 people, and much of daily life happens on property someone else is responsible for: the shopping centers strung along Elk Grove Boulevard and Laguna Boulevard, apartment complexes near Sheldon Road, restaurants, gyms, and office parks in every direction. When a floor is left slick, a stair rail is loose, or a walkway stays unlit, the person who falls is the one who pays for it first. California law puts the question this way: did the owner know, or should they have known, about the hazard, and did they fail to fix it or warn you? That word, notice, is where most premises cases in Sacramento County are won or lost. Photos of the spot, the names of anyone who saw it, and a prompt request that the business preserve its surveillance footage all matter more than people expect. LawProactive is not a law firm. We are a free service that connects Elk Grove residents with an independent personal injury attorney who works on contingency, so you owe nothing unless there is a recovery.

items.question: I slipped in a store off Elk Grove Boulevard but no employee saw it happen. Do I still have a case?
items.answer: Possibly. The question is not whether someone watched you fall, but whether the store knew or should have known about the hazard and failed to address it. Surveillance video, cleaning schedules, and prior complaints can establish that even without an eyewitness. Report the fall to the manager in writing as soon as you can so there is a record.

items.question: How long do I have to file a premises liability claim in California?
items.answer: Generally two years from the date of the injury. If the property belongs to a public entity, such as the City of Elk Grove or Sacramento County, you typically must file a government claim within six months before any lawsuit. Because the shorter deadline is easy to miss, it helps to speak with an attorney early.

items.question: The store says I was looking at my phone when I fell. Does that end my claim?
items.answer: No. California follows pure comparative fault, which means your recovery is reduced by whatever percentage of blame is assigned to you rather than eliminated. If a jury decided you were 20 percent at fault, you could still recover 80 percent of your damages. An attorney can evaluate how that rule applies to your situation.
